Adult Dusky farmerfish (Stegastes nigricans) defending a nesting territory exhibit a maximum recorded standard length of 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters], a size attained only by the oldest, most dominant individuals within the colony. This terminal length is considerably larger than the length at which reproductive maturation typically initiates, which has been determined from field collections and histological examination of gonadal tissue. Individuals in the population along the fringing reefs of Okinawa consistently achieve sexual development at a standard length of approximately 5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5 centimeters], a threshold that marks the onset of territorial behavior and nest acquisition. The ecological significance of this size at puberty relates to the intense competition for suitable nesting substrate; smaller males are rarely able to secure and defend a crevice or algal patch, effectively delaying their contribution to the next generation until they have attained sufficient body dimensions. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analysis indicate that this 5 centimeter milestone is reached during the second year of benthic life, following a pelagic larval duration of several weeks. The pronounced size difference between pubertal and ultimate individuals reflects continued indeterminate growth, a common pattern among territorial pomacentrids that allows dominant males to progressively increase their body size and reproductive success over many seasons.

At the water temperatures characteristic of their shallow reef habitat, typically recorded at 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], the yolk-sac larva emerges from the demersal egg after an incubation period of approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days]. This rapid embryonic development, which is mediated by the elevated thermal regime of tropical inshore waters, produces a newly hatched larva that is entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves. The size of the fertilised ovum, with an egg diameter of roughly 1 millimeter, dictates an initial wet weight at birth of about 0.00052 grams [Wwb = about 0.00052 grams]. This remarkably small mass, characteristic of pelagic-spawning teleosts, means the prolarva faces intense starvation pressure from the moment of chorion rupture. The onset of exogenous feeding must occur within a narrow window following yolk-sac resorption, or the larva will reach the point of no return. Field estimates of survival through this critical early larval bottleneck are exceedingly low, with mortality rates exceeding ninety percent during the first week of free-swimming life, underscoring the selective advantage of rapid developmental rates afforded by the consistently warm water column.

Reproductive output in the Dusky farmerfish has been quantified through direct observation of nesting males during the summer spawning season. Under the stable thermal regime of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C] that prevails during the peak breeding months, a single, actively spawning male can guard a nest containing up to 200 eggs deposited per day [Ri = up to 200 eggs deposited per day] by multiple visiting females. This maximum reproductive rate is sustained only when algal cover on the nesting substrate is dense and when the male is able to maintain constant vigilance against egg predators, particularly the wrasse Thalassoma hardwicke. The figure of up to 200 eggs deposited per day is derived from repeated in situ counts of newly laid, translucent eggs on the nest surface, with each batch being laid in a single layer among the cultivated algal turf. Females, which are smaller than the territorial males on average, visit several nests over the course of a daily spawning bout, distributing their clutch among multiple males to reduce the risk of total brood loss. This mating system, characterized by male territorial defense and female mate choice based on nest quality and male condition, is typical of the genus Stegastes.

The substantial investment in somatic growth over the lifespan of the Dusky farmerfish is reflected in the pronounced difference between the weight at puberty and the ultimate mass attained by senescent adults. At the onset of sexual maturation, an individual typically weighs approximately 3.1 grams [Wwp = approximately 3.1 grams], a mass that is adequate to support the metabolic demands of territory defense and gamete production. However, over the subsequent years of continued feeding and growth, the body weight increases more than twentyfold, ultimately reaching an ultimate wet weight of 69.4 grams [Wwi = 69.4 grams] in the largest territorial males. This asymptotic body mass is consistent with the length-weight relationship derived from a large sample of specimens collected across the species' range. The thirty-fold increase in wet weight from the 0.00052 gram [Wwb = 0.00052 gram] hatchling to the fully grown adult represents a dramatic ontogenetic trajectory. Such pronounced size variation within the population creates distinct ecological niches: the smaller, pubertal individuals are often relegated to peripheral, lower-quality territories, while the dominant, heavy males command the central nesting sites with the densest algal gardens.

Longevity records for Dusky farmerfish, based on mark-recapture studies conducted within a long-term monitoring plot on the reef slope, indicate a maximum lifespan of 9 years [am = 9 years] under the stable thermal conditions of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C] that characterize their environment. This lifespan is notably extended compared to several smaller-bodied damselfish congeners, suggesting that the species' large ultimate size and intense territorial behavior confer a survival advantage against predators. The oldest individuals, recognized by their worn fin rays and faded coloration, often exhibit reduced reproductive activity in their final year, consistent with a pattern of gradual reproductive senescence. The age-based mortality rate remains relatively low for the first five years of adult life but increases sharply thereafter, with very few fish surviving beyond their eighth year. This longevity, coupled with the high annual fecundity of dominant males, means that a small number of old, large individuals contribute disproportionately to the overall reproductive output of the local population. The life history strategy of Stegastes nigricans thus appears to balance a moderate to high adult survival rate against the substantial energetic costs of year-round territory maintenance and continuous spawning during the summer months.
